source.title: Sparsity Moves Computation: How FFN Architecture Reshapes Attention in Small Transformers

page_placements.theme: Architecture and training-time constraints (activation or weight sparsity, LWTA/TopK, decorrelation, concept supervision, gating, activation function, weight decay, non-negativity, write-disjoint experts, ViT vs ResNet) change neuron monosemanticity

record.tranche_reason: The study measures architecture-dependent neuron-level Fourier structure and whether PCA or a weight-based analysis recovers structure, bearing conceptually on V4. It does not use the original neuron-pole job audit or explanation-testing method.
record.gate_note: The paper studies one-layer transformers on algorithmic tasks, not the claim’s neuron-pole job categories. Its Fourier concentrations and subspace analyses are relevant proxies for how visible task structure is at the neuron level, but do not measure the share of neurons with one or more named jobs. It reports no test of the other claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. Its main result is that MoE sparsity shifts computation from the FFN to attention in one-layer transformers trained on algorithmic tasks. Its secondary GLU result uses mean per-neuron Fourier concentration and PCA or weight-space concentration. These are frequency-selectivity proxies, not a share of neurons with an explained job. No version names Fourier selectivity in toy algorithmic models, so the GLU finding goes under fits_no_version. The study does not cite the essay or Bills et al. The record's 'supports' label for V4 also reverses the logic. PCA and weight-space analysis find structure outside the neuron basis, which says better non-neuron tools reveal what neurons hide. V4 says better tools raise the share of interpretable neurons.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate for the GLU part, but that is the paper's secondary finding. The main conclusion is about MoE routing. Sparse MoE routing shifts computation from the FFN to attention, most strongly on add-7. This comes from reduced per-token capacity plus sparse partitioning. Frozen random routing nearly matches learned routing. Separately, GLU gating rotates Fourier structure out of the per-neuron basis into distributed subspaces, which makes neuron-level tools less informative.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses Fourier concentration, PCA, weight-based bilinear analysis, and algorithmic-task models rather than neuron-pole explanations tested on held-out activating examples.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured visibility of Fourier structure depends on representation and analysis level: per-neuron concentration is low for GLU-family models, while PCA and weight-based measures recover structure. The add-7 width control also compares GLU with dense models of matched neuron count.

fits_no_version.finding: In parameter-matched one-layer transformers on mod-113 addition, GLU and MoE-GLU cut mean per-neuron Fourier concentration (0.17 and 0.16, versus 0.34 for FFN). PCA and weight-space bilinear analysis still recover Fourier structure. The paper attributes the drop to the multiplicative gate, not to neuron count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multiplicative (GLU) gating, the standard in modern LLMs, lowers per-neuron selectivity for task features relative to plain FFNs. Structure stays recoverable in low-dimensional subspaces or weights, so neuron-level inspection understates the computation.

record.problems: The evidence comes from small one-layer transformers trained on algorithmic tasks, not language models or vision models. Fourier concentration and subspace recovery are proxies for neuron-level interpretability, not counts of interpretable neurons or named jobs. Some component values are reported for a single checkpoint, and the paper does not test explanation prediction on held-out activations.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant results were omitted. Component ablations, routing, task accuracy, and grokking results were left out because they do not measure the neuron-level interpretability or architecture/tool claims in V4.

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit and its shares of one-job, two-job and not-understood poles.
Shares across language models, dense and MoE, and across scale.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose, recursive generalization versus superposition.
Share of interpretable neurons as a function of architecture, regularization and tools. Vision-model estimates. Late-layer neurons.
Neuron-based attribution graphs, replacement models, reconstruction error.
Whether explanations fitted to activating examples predict held-out firing.
Simulation-based automated scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The study does not cite the essay or Bills et al. Its setting is tiny one-layer models on algorithmic tasks. If a curator still wanted a link to V4, the GLU result would at most limit the scope of the 'modern architectures' clause: GLU lowered per-neuron selectivity here. It would not support V4; the record's 'supports' label is backwards. No instructions were found in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B pole audit and the proportions with one job, two related jobs, or not-yet-understood poles.
Similar pole-job shares across language models, dense and MoE models, or model scales.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose detection, recursive generalization, and superposition.

The study does not count interpretable neurons or estimate an interpretable share; it does not study Inception-sized vision models, late layers, regularization effects, or comparisons among explanation tools. Its PCA and weight-based analyses examine recovery of Fourier structure in small algorithmic models.
Attribution graphs, behavior reconstruction, replacement models, and reconstruction error.
Whether explanations fit to activating examples predict where a neuron fires on held-out activations.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by predicting activations on new text.

relation.reason: The paper does not cite or use the claim. Its GLU section discusses whether neurons are a privileged basis for interpretation, which is the claim's topic.

tranche.reason: Per-neuron Fourier concentration, PCA and weight bilinear analysis on toy algorithmic models measure frequency selectivity, not a share of neurons with one main job. This is a related but different construct, so no version is tested.

source_check.notes: All 11 rows match the text. Per-neuron Fourier concentration is a frequency-selectivity proxy, not an interpretable-neuron share. GLU lowering per-neuron legibility is the result nearest to V4, but it is on a different construct (fits_no_version). Fig. 22 / App. B give 0.07 (GLU) and 0.18 (MoE-GLU) as per-neuron values 'on the same checkpoints'. These differ from Table 5 (0.17/0.16), and the paper does not explain the difference.

statements.correction: Numbers match Fig. 5 / Tables 5-6 (modadd, total-parameter-matched, 5 seeds, GELU default): GLU 0.17, MoE-GLU 0.16, FFN 0.34 (±0.13, one outlier seed at 0.09; other four average about 0.40). Plain MoE is 0.48. PCA: GLU top-1 PC 0.49 vs FFN 0.41. Weight-based bilinear: 0.38 (GLU), 0.39 (MoE-GLU).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: GLU-family models on modular addition and the add-7 width control
reader_labels.reason: Per-neuron Fourier concentration is lower for GLU and MoE-GLU than for FFN, while the paper says task structure remains present; this cautions against treating neuron-level visibility as architecture-independent (r2, r4, r19, r25).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: PCA and weight-based analyses of GLU-family models on modular addition
reader_labels.reason: PCA concentration and weight-based concentration reveal Fourier structure despite low per-neuron concentration, consistent with analysis method affecting what structure is recovered (r6, r10, r21, r22).
